# Hard-to-vary report: Hume, "Of the Idea of Necessary Connexion"

**1. The question, frozen.**
The section answers more than one question, but the title and the opening pick the central one: *where does our idea of "power, force, energy, or necessary connexion" come from — from what impression is it copied?* Range: every case of cause and effect, in bodies and in minds. Kind: a source question — what produces the idea. (The section also asks whether God is the immediate cause of every event. I treat that as the rival, in section 4.)

**2. The explanation in parts.**
- P1 Every idea is a copy of an impression; no impression, no idea.
- P2 Watching bodies, we see one event follow another; the senses never show a tie.
- P3 Looking inward, we feel no power in the will — over body or over mind.
- P4 One instance gives no such idea; many similar ones do.
- P5 The one thing many instances have that a single one lacks is the mind's habit — its customary glide from an object to its usual attendant.
- P6 That felt glide is the impression the idea is copied from.
- P7 Two definitions of cause: constant conjunction; the felt transition.
- (R) Rival: God's volition is the immediate cause of every event.

Jobs, each as a contrast, with origin: why we have the idea at all (given); why one instance gives none and many do (given); why we infer the effect from the cause (added by Hume); why the idea is not in bodies (given by the search); why it is not in the will (added); why the occasionalists are wrong (added).

**3. Part by part.**

| Part | Mark | Why |
|---|---|---|
| P1 copy principle | **borrowed** | Rests on Section II's argument, not tested here. |
| P2 senses show only succession | **held** | By the job "why a single instance gives no idea," and the poke: strike two balls; only one following another shows. |
| P3 no power felt in the will | **held** | By two pokes: the paralytic wills an unmovable limb and feels the same "power"; anatomy shows the will moves muscles it never aimed at. |
| P4 many instances, not one | **held** | By the contrast it was built for. |
| P5 habit is the sole difference | **held** | Remove it and nothing tells many instances from one. |
| P6 the felt glide is the impression | **held** | Remove it and, given P1, the idea has no source left. |
| P7 the two definitions | **two routes** | Each answers "what is cause": the first names the conjunction, the second the felt transition. Neither is needed alone. |
| "some secret mechanism or structure of parts" inside the will | **loose** (a catch-all with no gauge) | It swallows how the will works. Allowed only with a reading that would show it swallowing a job. |

**4. Whole-explanation checks.**
- **Flip.** Had a single instance shown a tie, or had we plainly felt power in the will, the explanation breaks — and Hume says so. It does not fit both outcomes.
- **Direction.** Mostly backward: from the idea we have, back to the source it must have. But it commits forward: the felt glide *produces* the idea. The test is whether poking the glide moves the idea.
- **Answer hidden in the starting points?** "Habit" looks like a relabel of the phenomenon — until P5 earns it by being the sole difference between one instance and many. Without P5, it is circular.
- **Jobs.** Hume's own added jobs (inference, the will's limits, the occasionalists) each rule out a rival. They pull weight.
- **Pairs that pull.** P1 pulls against R: if we can have no idea of a power we never felt, "God's volition" has no content. Hume uses exactly this pull.
- **Change list leaves out, openly:** no experiment reaches a tie; and the workings of habit itself.
- **Rival.** Hume builds the occasionalist case properly — God moves the second ball, God joins soul and body — then knocks it with P2/P3: we are as ignorant of a mind's power as of a body's. A fair, strong rival, not a straw one.
- **Provenance.** P1 borrowed (Hume argued it elsewhere); P2–P6 built, worked out with the thing in view; P7 fitted to the two patterns already found.

**5. What would make it harder to vary.**
Two pokes cut deepest. First: find a single instance that conveys the idea of power — that kills P4. Second: find a felt power that survives the nerve being cut — that kills P3. Either forces a rebuild rather than a patch.

**6. What this does not show.**
Hard to vary is not the same as true. The copy principle and the felt-glide move carry their own load elsewhere; passing here settles neither.

**7. One next step.**
Test P1 on a case it never met: an idea with no matching impression — a shade of colour never seen but imagined. If one exists, P1 loosens, and P6 needs a different anchor.
